newsitem.title: ITALY: Gucci's ex-wife "too distraught" to talk.
newsitem.headline: Gucci's ex-wife "too distraught" to talk.

text.p: The ex-wife of slain Italian fashion heir Maurizio Gucci was too distraught to speak on Tuesday when investigators tried to question her in jail about suspicions that she ordered his killing, the woman's lawyer said.
Lawyer Marco De Luca said his client, Patrizia Reggiani Martinelli, was mentally and physically shattered.
"We shall see in the next few days whether her mental and physical condition is up to her answering questions. At the moment she isn't lucid enough," he told reporters.
Public prosecutor Carlo Nocerino, who had hoped to question Reggiani, left Milan's bleak San Vittore jail where Reggiani is being held on remand after less than an hour.
Reggiani, who had an acriminous 12-year marriage to Gucci, was arrested last Friday on suspicion that she paid contract killers $300,000 to murder her former husband.
Four other people are also under arrest, including Reggiani's "spiritual adviser" Giuseppina Auriemma.
Auriemma and hotel concierge Ivano Savioni are accused of brokering the contract and two men are accused of carrying out the shooting.
Maurizio Gucci, 45, was shot dead in broad daylight in March 1995 outside his office in central Milan.

The Gucci empire, with its unmistakable red and green motif and intertwined gilt GG logo, grew from a humble saddlery shop in Florence in 1906 into purveyors of luxury leather, luggage, shoes, ties and couture to the rich and famous.

Maurizio, the last grandson of founder Guccio Gucci, was plunged into feuds in the style of the Medicis of mediaeval Florence after inheriting his father's 50 percent share. The company is no longer associated with the family.

De Luca said he had so far been unable to mount a defence because of Reggiani's state. He has bitterly criticised lurid details of the investigation splashed across the Italian press since last week's arrests.
The "Dallas" tone of the coverage gave way on Tuesday to stories more reminiscent of the Hollywood gangster movie "Pulp Fiction".
Newspapers said an undercover Italian policeman who took part in the investigation had duped Savioni into believing he was a killer for a Colombian drugs baron.
"This is Carlos. He solves problems," was the way La Repubblica newspaper said the unidentified Spanish-speaking policeman had been introduced to Savioni.
"Carlos", according to the reports, told Savioni he had wiped out 120 people for a drugs lord called Hermann.
"I put a diamond on my little finger and wore a gold chain and open silk shirt. You know, the sort of clothing you'd imagine," La Repubblica quoted the agent as saying.
"It ended up with Savioni offering me his car to go out to dinner and we took the chance to stuff it with bugs," the agent said.
